one_liner: Rust no_std Wasm 3.0 runtime with interpreter and on-device JIT; interpreter about 1.9x WAMR fast-interp on wasmi-benchmarks.
what_it_does: Silverfir-nano is a WebAssembly runtime published as the sf-nano-core crate (0.6.0 on crates.io since 2026-09-09) with two engines behind one Rust API: a build-time-generated interpreter that needs no executable memory, and an optimizing JIT that compiles on the target itself, down to Cortex-M33 and RV32 microcontrollers. Embedding is Engine::new(Config) then Instance::new(&engine, wasm, &imports) and instance.call / invoke; Config::tier or Cargo features (jit, interp, guard-pages, wasi) pick the engine, and WASI preview1 is an optional feature. It is not API-compatible with WAMR's C API or wasmtime's, so switching means rewriting the host binding layer.
how_it_is_fast: The interpreter is a 'folded stack machine': a predecode pass folds Wasm operand-stack traffic into handlers that address 8-byte frame slots directly, and build.rs generates the whole dispatch engine as one global_asm! blob (about 10,300 handler variants specialised by operand class, including pinned-register locals, address-fused loads/stores and pair moves) with absolute branch targets and a hot-families-first emission order. The JIT lowers Wasm to Semantic IR, SSA-IR, MachineIR and native code, gives locals and deep stack values fixed frame-slot homes so only short-lived transients need register allocation, and uses a region-based cache-residency allocator (docs/ALGORITHM4.md) plus late peepholes (addressing-mode fusion, load/store forwarding, branch fusion); guard pages let it elide bounds checks.
when_to_use: You need a pure interpreter (W^X platforms, no executable memory, smallest flash) and want the fastest one measured: wasmi-benchmarks execute geomean on AMD EPYC 7763 is 9.02 vs Wasmi v2 12.40, Wasm3 16.51 and WAMR fast-interp 17.07 (lower is better), and it was the fastest interpreter on all five machines in that suite (M2 Pro, M4 Pro, i7700, Xeon 8573C, EPYC).

Microcontroller deployments where you ship a .wasm and want either tier on chip: recorded RP2350 firmware is 337 KiB flash with the interpreter and about 1,042 KiB with the JIT, on Cortex-M33 and Hazard3 RV32, plus an ESP32-C6 port.

Apple Silicon hosts that want Cranelift-class compiled throughput from a small no_std crate: its JIT had the best execute geomean of all 23 configurations on Apple M2 Pro (1.06) and M4 Pro (1.07) in wasmi-benchmarks.
Products that need one runtime across x86_64, ARM64, RV64, RV32, ARMv7-A and Thumb-2 with the same embedding API for interpreter and JIT.
when_not_to_use: x86-64 throughput-bound hosts: the JIT trails Cranelift and V8 there (wasmi-benchmarks execute geomean EPYC 7763 1.25 vs 1.15 and 1.05; i7700 1.46 vs 1.25 and 1.13; Xeon 8573C 1.28 vs 1.21 and 1.04), and the first-party Apple M4 table has Cranelift winning 9 of 15 metrics.

Startup-dominated workloads on the interpreter: its eager predecode makes startup geomean 61.98 on EPYC vs WAMR 56.73, Wasm3 (eager) 51.60 and Wasmi v2 (lazy) 1.37, so Wasmi's lazy modes start far faster.
Modules that use SIMD or GC on the interpreter (refused at instantiation by design), or SIMD on the RV and ARMv7 JIT backends (JIT SIMD needs ARM64 NEON or x86_64 SSSE3+SSE4.1).
C or C++ hosts: only a Rust API is documented, unlike WAMR and wasm3.

Teams needing a long production record: 67 stars, 29 crates.io downloads, a single maintainer, a 0.x API, and design notes (docs/decisions.json) still consolidating about 19 raw *mut Store dereferences into one audited checkout primitive; no fuzzing setup is mentioned in the docs read.

integration.form: crate (sf-nano-core; cargo features jit, interp, guard-pages, wasi; defaults jit+interp+guard-pages)
integration.dependencies: sf-nano-tracked-alloc (same repository); optional filetime for wasi; needs alloc; bare-metal JIT embedders must supply executable-memory and instruction-cache hooks
integration.platforms: x86_64, ARM64, RV64, RV32, ARMv7-A, Thumb-2 for both engines; CI runs x64 Linux, ARM64 Linux, ARM64 macOS and x64 Windows MSVC natively, ARMv7/RV64/RV32 under QEMU, and builds bare-metal thumbv8m and RV32IMAC
integration.thread_safety: not documented; memory views are exclusive within a RuntimeWorld and design notes describe Rc-shared internals, so treat an engine and its instances as single-threaded; eager JIT compilation of large modules is spread over multiple threads by default (Config::parallel_compilation)

gotchas: Interpreter scores depend on where its handlers land in memory: docs/HANDLER_LAYOUT.md records 48 bytes of unreachable padding moving x64-windows sha256 from -14.83% to +0.27% and arm64-linux STREAM Scale by +103.49%. The fix (pinned 64-byte phase boundaries) landed 2026-08-01, after the 2026-07-25 interpreter column in RESULTS.md, so its micro-kernel rows (sha256, STREAM, CoreMark) may include layout luck in either direction.

The first-party wasmi column is disputed: in issue #11 (2026-07-27) the wasmi author said the CoreMark numbers looked like wasmi 1.0.9 rather than 2.0.0-beta.7 and that on Apple Silicon Wasm3 and Wasmi beta.7 CoreMark are very close. The issue was closed with no visible reply, and the CoreMark interpreter row was later replaced by standalone scores (wasmi beta.10), so that row mixes measurement modes. Interpreters are single runs, and the wasm3 build is unpinned.

Harness asymmetries in RESULTS.md: wasmtime 47 returns 0.0 from Lua's os.clock(), so the Lua rows on wasmtime used a 1-second os.time() fallback while other engines used the high-resolution path; the sqlite row is historical speedtest1 data that the current suite no longer runs.

Engine limits: the JIT once failed to instantiate the SpiderMonkey startup module on Linux and Windows ('linear-value budget exhausted during cache alias materialization', issue #10, fixed in PR #16). The JIT passes host-thrown exceptions to the embedder even when Wasm declares a handler. Interpreter host functions return at most eight results. Module::new_unchecked is unsafe.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over Wasmi, Wasm3, Stitch or the WAMR fast interpreter when execution speed of a pure interpreter matters most and the modules need no SIMD or GC: it led every interpreter on all five wasmi-benchmarks machines. Pick Wasmi (lazy) for startup-bound or many-short-lived-instance workloads, and WAMR or Wasm3 when you need a C API and a longer production record.
verified_claims_summary: In the wasmi-benchmarks suite, run by the wasmi author (a competitor) on an AMD EPYC 7763 with Silverfir-nano tag 0.5, the Silverfir interpreter's execute geomean is 9.02x the fastest runtime per case, against 17.07x for WAMR fast-interp, 16.51x for Wasm3 and 12.40x for Wasmi v2. That makes it about 1.9x faster than WAMR and 1.37x faster than Wasmi (derived from page data). Its JIT is 1.25x vs Cranelift 1.15x and V8 1.05x on that machine, but leads on Apple M2 Pro and M4 Pro. The first-party Apple M4 suite (wasi-sdk clang -O2 guests, Silverfir LTO opt-level 3) puts the interpreter 1.07-1.69x ahead of the better of Wasm3 and Wasmi per row and the JIT at parity with wasmtime 47.0.2 Cranelift.
status_note: Actively developed by one maintainer (1,306 commits, last commit 2026-10-03, crates.io 0.6.0 on 2026-09-09) under MIT OR Apache-2.0, usable as a crate today, but young and not yet hardened for hostile modules.
